title: The oldest Marian prayer
hookLine: Sub tuum praesidium, found on an ancient papyrus: we fly to thy protection

lines: A SCRAP OF PAPYRUS, IN GREEK.
cards: A scrap of papyrus, written in Greek, torn at the edges, with only parts of its lines left. Someone wrote a few words of prayer on it, and when scholars pieced them together, they matched a prayer the Church still says.
In Latin it begins Sub tuum praesidium; in the traditional English, we fly to thy protection, O holy Mother of God. No grand liturgy around it. No author's name.
Just a handful of people, it seems, in some kind of trouble, running toward a mother.

teach.h: A NICKNAME WITH A QUESTION MARK.
teach.b: First, the nickname, and its question mark. People call this the oldest Marian prayer. Scholars argue about how old the papyrus is, and the argument isn't settled, so it's fair to hold the nickname loosely.
What nobody needs to argue about is what the prayer says. Second, the picture.
We fly to thy protection: fly here means flee, run for cover. It's the posture of the psalm about God's shelter, which in the Douay-Rheims says, "under his wings thou shalt trust."
The prayer doesn't stand up straight and make a speech. It ducks under cover.

Third, the name it calls her: Holy Mother of God, the first of the four teachings that opened this stretch on Mary. Here it isn't an argument in a council or a line in a creed. It's what people shout when they're running.

teach.h: IT NEVER SAYS I. IT SAYS WE.
teach.b: The prayer never says I. Despise not our petitions in our necessities, it goes on, but deliver us always from all dangers, O glorious and blessed Virgin.
A group of people with real needs and real dangers, praying together.

teach.h: UNDER HIS WINGS THOU SHALT TRUST.
teach.b: And it's still said: in Latin in the West, and in Greek and other languages in Eastern churches, at evening prayer and at the end of the rosary. Short enough for one breath. Old enough that its own age is a question.
And plural, so whoever says it today says it with everyone who ever ran for the same shelter.

how: Catholics pray the Sub tuum praesidium in Latin or English, sometimes at the end of the rosary or of Night Prayer, and Eastern Christians sing it in their own languages at evening services.

games.q: danger is close, and there's no time for a long prayer. what does this one do?
o: list the reasons it deserves help.
run for cover: we fly to thy protection.
wait until things calm down to pray properly.
games.why: it ducks under shelter, all together: we fly to thy protection, O holy Mother of God... deliver us always from all dangers.

practice: Bring to mind a few people in danger or need right now, someone sick, someone in a war zone, someone who can't pay the rent, and gather them into one small group, the way the prayer says we.

If you pray, say the Sub tuum praesidium once, slowly, for all of you together: we fly to thy protection, O holy Mother of God. If you don't, hold that group in mind as if you were all under one roof in a storm.

wordCard.voice: The oldest Marian prayer. The nickname of the Sub tuum praesidium, found on a Greek papyrus: we fly to thy protection, O holy Mother of God.

orig.note: Latin: under thy protection we take refuge, the prayer's opening; the papyrus is in Greek.

carryVoice: Your line: we fly to thee. Never I, always we. That's today, done.
